newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean troops, mobs in witch hunt for Tutsis.
newsitem.headline: Zairean troops, mobs in witch hunt for Tutsis.

text.p: Drunk and loaded with an assortment of weapons, Zairean troops set up barricades in the Zairean town of Bukavu in a witch hunt for ethnic Tutsis.

Hundreds of civilians gathered on Thursday to watch the spectacle of the notoriously ill-disciplined Zairean army at work after authorities gave an estimated 200,000 Banyamulenge Tutsis until next week to leave.
The ultimatum for the Banyamulenge to leave or be hunted down as rebels changed little in military terms, but gave civilians and soldiers licence to start an open-season against ethnic Tutsis.
Even non-Banyamulenge were caught up in the rising spiral of popular hatred against the ethnic Tutsis, who are denied Zairean nationality despite arriving in the area up to 200 years ago.

A total of 35 Banyamulenge were executed extrajudicially by Zairean authorities in September and more than 50 others disappeared, according to reports received by London-based human rights group Amnesty International.

Banyamulenge, economically richer than other ethnic groups in the area, have been all but driven from Bukavu and Uvira towns and most now live on the high plateau northwest of Lake Tanganyika. Around 500 Banyamulenge have fled to Rwanda in recent weeks and hundreds of others have fled to Burundi.
I arrived in Bukavu on Tuesday on an aid flight from Kenya and within one hour residents tipped off Zairean state security that I, a tall, black British journalist, was a suspected Banyamulenge.

State security agents and soldiers picked me up from a hotel. I was arrested, strip-searched, locked in a small cell after my shoes and socks had been confiscated and screamed at by a guard wielding a crowbar.
Only the intervention of U.N. officials and the deputy governor of south Kivu province secured my release after nearly an hour. The soldiers who had arrested me saw no reason to apologise.
On Wednesday morning a group of foreign journalists watched as a contingent of Zairean soldiers prepared to give us a military escort to the troubled town of Uvira, south of Bukavu.

Soldiers ordered an aid agency employee to hand over the keys to two pickup trucks at gunpoint and loaded them with an assortment of weapons including rocket-propelled grenade launchers, a cannon, machineguns and hundreds of rounds of ammunition.
One of the soldiers then decided I might be a Banyamulenge.
Showing my British passport and other documents made no difference and the beginnings of an ugly scene developed because the soldiers were apparently more after blood than money.

The soldiers who had been ordered to release me the previous day did nothing to intervene and the deputy governor's personal envoy, detailed to guarantee the journalists' security, could not stop his own troops making the arrest.
A senior officer, educated in the United States, secured my release.
"These people are little more than animals, especially when they start drinking," he said of his own men.
"While I'm here there's nothing they can do, but if you let them escort you to Uvira you will arrive there but your head will be left behind on the road somewhere." I pulled out of the trip.

There is very little logic to the persecution of ethnic Tutsis. Ordinary citizens, all too willing to believe political propaganda, can denounce anyone to authorities as Banyamulenge to pay back old scores or out of economic jealousy.
Soldiers, who complain about being poorly and irregularly paid, stop cars at random if they want money and take it. But a suspected Banyamulenge may find them impossible to pay off.
